claims.text: Adding a thermally stable solid-lubricant phase to CoCrFeNi will reduce its coefficient of friction from room temperature to 800 °C relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi.
Adding a thermally stable solid-lubricant phase to CoCrFeNi will reduce its wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi.
MoS2 or hexagonal boron nitride could serve as the thermally stable solid-lubricant phase in this system.
The solid-lubricant phase can be introduced into CoCrFeNi through in situ synthesis or mechanical alloying.
The intervention will produce a solid-lubricant phase dispersed within the CoCrFeNi matrix.
The dispersed solid-lubricant phase will enable formation of a tribofilm during sliding.
The resulting tribofilm will have low shear strength.
The tribofilm will reduce direct metal-to-metal contact at the sliding interface.
Reduced interfacial shear strength and metal-to-metal contact will lower friction and wear.
Thermal stability of the lubricant phase will maintain its effectiveness throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The modified alloy will have a coefficient of friction at least 30% lower than unmodified CoCrFeNi across the full temperature range.
The modified alloy will have a wear rate at least 40% lower than unmodified CoCrFeNi across the full temperature range.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi exhibits higher friction and wear, especially at elevated temperatures.
The proposed effectiveness applies in dry air from room temperature to 800 °C and under loads of 1–10 N.
If the lubricant phase oxidizes, decomposes, or becomes depleted, tribological performance will revert to the unmodified-alloy baseline.
The degree of friction and wear reduction depends on the stability and distribution of the solid-lubricant phase.
Failure of the lubricant phase to form a tribofilm may eliminate the effectiveness of the intervention.
